title: Grand Theft Auto VI writer behind female protagonist deletes X account after online hate
summary: One of the writers behind Grand Theft Auto VI has had to delete her X account after facing online backlash for her role in writing the game's female protagonist, Lucia Caminos. Alexa D’Agostino…

image.caption: Lucia Caminos is one of two leads that make up the Bonnie and Clyde duo in Grand Theft Auto VI. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

One of the writers behind Grand Theft Auto VI has had to delete her X account after facing online backlash for her role in writing the game's female protagonist, Lucia Caminos. Alexa D’Agostino became the subject of an online harassment campaign.
Alexa D’Agostino worked on the character Lucia Caminos for the new billion-dollar game
One of the writers behind Grand Theft Auto VI has had to delete her X account after facing online backlash for her role in writing the game's female protagonist, Lucia Caminos.
Alexa D’Agostino became the subject of an online harassment campaign that highlighted some of her past blog posts around dating and posts she shared on X.

D’Agostino is one of three people credited for writing the narrative of Grand Theft Auto VI, a game that quickly became one the biggest video games of all time, making a record-setting $3.79 billion US in day one retail sales.
The game allows players to play as Jason and Lucia, a Bonnie and Clyde-type duo that steal and shoot their way through the fictional state of Leonida, based on Florida.
But the game has also come with some backlash, as some streamers have labelled the game as too woke, referring specifically to the relationship between the two protagonists.
Writing a female lead

Before deleting her X account, D’Agostino had been posting on social media about the game and sharing clips of its gameplay. Ahead of the release, she talked about how Lucia was inspired by the women in her life.
"My mother was an immigrant who grew up in Newark, New Jersey," D'Agostino told Love Magazine.
"I thought about the way she raised me: rowdy, kind, but not to take any shit. I related a lot to Lucia, and writing her came very naturally to me."
Alexa D’Agostino has talked about the inspirations for writing Lucia Caminos, but her comments have garnered backlash from some gamers. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)
D'Agostino hoped Lucia would compare to lead characters from other Rockstar Games properties, such as Red Dead Redemption 2 and Grand Theft Auto IV.

"When you are focusing on writing a fully realized person with their own wants, you’re going to get something perfectly imperfect — with clichés, but also undeniably real. That’s how you get a woman that can stand tall next to the likes of Arthur Morgan and Niko Bellic."
Hateful comments

Following the game's release, D'Agostino was harassed on social media. Some of the comments claimed she gave advice for manipulating men in a 2015 blog post titled "Do's and Dont's when meeting his friends."

"They were finding old writing that she did and combing her profile to try and [say], 'Oh, of course she wrote about how you can manipulate and take advantage of men and that's why GTA is woke,'" said Alyssa Mercante, a culture critic and gaming journalist.
In D'Agostino's post, she suggests asking people questions about themselves, knowing what you're getting into and being yourself.
People also attacked her for things like sharing a post wishing people a happy Pride month.
One user posted on X claiming a D'Agostino blog post about meeting your boyfriend's friends is advice on 'how to manipulate and take advantage of men.' (X)
"The person writing video games you and your family buy to enjoy and cool down," said @cheetos687 on X.
Another gamer posted on Facebook saying, "No wonder the game flopped so hard."

D'Agostino deleted her account earlier this week. CBC reached out to Rockstar Games for comment on how it handles online backlash targeting one of its employees. Rockstar Games did not respond before publication.
Part of a cycle
According to Mercante, this type of backlash is part of a cycle from a particular community of gamers.

"It's a very popular tactic that has been deployed for the last couple of years in this space, where they find people who work on games, identify them, share their social profiles and harass them," she said.
"These are targeted harassments campaigns where they ensure that they dehumanize and demonize the target."
Mercante says that often the biggest voices in the space won't directly tell people to harass others, but will point out someone and then list all of their social media accounts.
"It is implied," said Mercante.

When Ghost of Yōtei came out in 2025, some players weren't happy that the lead character was a woman. Then, when one of the artists for the game made a comment about the assassination of popular U.S. conservative activist Charlie Kirk, people came at her online, calling for the game studio to fire her. After repeated calls for her termination, she was eventually fired from that job, though Sony didn't say specifically the reason for it.
Mercante said much of this backlash comes down to monetization, as streamers and influencers make money based on how many views and clicks they get.
"The current creator culture in this space, and the way that social media has been set up and monetized over the last few years, requires a regular villain of the day."
